title: Early human activity (About 709,000 years ago)
content:
About 709,000 years ago: Early human activity. Stone tools and rhinoceros bones bearing cut marks, excavated in Kalinga, provide evidence of early hominin activity in Luzon. The species responsible has not been identified.
Source: https://www.nationalmuseum.gov.ph/our-collections/archaeology/archeology-division-history/ (listed 2026-11-19).

title: The Tabon Cave discoveries (Tens of thousands of years ago)
content:
Tens of thousands of years ago: The Tabon Cave discoveries. Excavations at the Tabon Cave Complex in Palawan uncovered early Homo sapiens remains and evidence of toolmaking and burial practices. Finds from different periods help researchers study the long human history of the islands.
Source: https://www.nationalmuseum.gov.ph/our-collections/archaeology/archeology-division-history/ (listed 2026-11-19).

title: Laguna Copperplate Inscription (900 CE)
content:
900 CE: Laguna Copperplate Inscription. This copperplate records the settlement of a debt. Its language and script show connections between communities in the archipelago and the wider trading world of Southeast Asia.
Source: https://ncca.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/PHILIPPINE-HISTORY-SOURCE-BOOK-FINAL-SEP022021.pdf (listed 2026-11-19).

title: Islam and the southern sultanates (14th–15th centuries)
content:
14th–15th centuries: Islam and the southern sultanates. Islam spread through trade and religious networks in the southern islands. Muslim communities and, later, sultanates became important centers of political, commercial and religious life.
Source: https://ncca.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/PHILIPPINE-HISTORY-SOURCE-BOOK-FINAL-SEP022021.pdf (listed 2026-11-19).

title: Magellan’s expedition and Mactan (1521)
content:
1521: Magellan’s expedition and Mactan. The expedition led by Ferdinand Magellan reached the archipelago while sailing for Spain. Magellan died at Mactan in a battle with forces led by Lapulapu. Permanent Spanish settlement began decades later.
Source: https://ncca.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/PHILIPPINE-HISTORY-SOURCE-BOOK-FINAL-SEP022021.pdf (listed 2026-11-19).

title: Spanish settlement and administration (1565–1571)
content:
1565–1571: Spanish settlement and administration. Miguel López de Legazpi established a Spanish settlement in Cebu in 1565. Manila became the colonial capital in 1571. Spanish administration expanded unevenly across the islands, alongside communities that maintained their independence.
Source: https://ncca.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/PHILIPPINE-HISTORY-SOURCE-BOOK-FINAL-SEP022021.pdf (listed 2026-11-19).

title: Philippine Revolution (1896)
content:
1896: Philippine Revolution. The Katipunan, founded in 1892 with Andrés Bonifacio among its organizers, began an armed revolution against Spanish colonial rule. The conflict led to revolutionary governments and the declaration of independence in 1898.
Source: https://philhistoricsites.nhcp.gov.ph/registry_database/site-of-the-proclamation-of-philippine-independence/ (listed 2026-11-19).

metadata.licence: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, BetterGov.ph; adapted for Kuya J with permission

title: Declaration of independence (12 June 1898)
content:
12 June 1898: Declaration of independence. Philippine independence was proclaimed at Emilio Aguinaldo’s home in Kawit, Cavite. The Philippine flag was displayed and Julián Felipe’s march, which became the national anthem, was performed.
Source: https://philhistoricsites.nhcp.gov.ph/registry_database/site-of-the-proclamation-of-philippine-independence/ (listed 2026-11-19).

title: Treaty of Paris and the Philippine-American War (1898–1902)
content:
1898–1902: Treaty of Paris and the Philippine-American War. Under the Treaty of Paris, Spain ceded the Philippines to the United States. Filipino forces contested American sovereignty, and war began in 1899. Although the United States declared the war ended in 1902, armed resistance continued in some areas.
Source: https://history.house.gov/Exhibitions-and-Publications/APA/Historical-Essays/Exclusion-and-Empire/The-Philippines/ (listed 2026-11-19).

metadata.licence: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, BetterGov.ph; adapted for Kuya J with permission

title: Commonwealth inaugurated (15 November 1935)
content:
15 November 1935: Commonwealth inaugurated. Following the 1934 Tydings–McDuffie Act, the Commonwealth was inaugurated as a transitional government toward independence. Manuel L. Quezon served as its first president.
Source: https://history.house.gov/Exhibitions-and-Publications/APA/Historical-Essays/Exclusion-and-Empire/The-Philippines/ (listed 2026-11-19).

metadata.licence: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, BetterGov.ph; adapted for Kuya J with permission

title: War and Japanese occupation (1941–1945)
content:
1941–1945: War and Japanese occupation. Japan invaded in December 1941. The occupation brought widespread loss of life and destruction, including the Bataan Death March and the Battle of Manila. Filipino guerrillas and Allied forces fought in the campaign to end the occupation.
Source: https://history.house.gov/Exhibitions-and-Publications/APA/Historical-Essays/Exclusion-and-Empire/The-Philippines/ (listed 2026-11-19).

title: Independence recognized (4 July 1946)
content:
4 July 1946: Independence recognized. The United States recognized Philippine independence, and Manuel Roxas became president of the Third Republic. The annual Independence Day observance later shifted to June 12 to commemorate the 1898 declaration.
Source: https://history.house.gov/Exhibitions-and-Publications/APA/Historical-Essays/Exclusion-and-Empire/The-Philippines/ (listed 2026-11-19).

title: Declaration of martial law (1972–1981)
content:
1972–1981: Declaration of martial law. President Ferdinand E. Marcos placed the Philippines under martial law through Proclamation No. 1081, dated 21 September 1972, citing rebellion and threats to public order. The period brought expanded presidential powers, restrictions on the press and civil liberties, and documented human rights violations. Martial law was formally lifted on 17 January 1981 through Proclamation No. 2045; Marcos remained president until February 1986.
Source: https://lawphil.net/executive/proc/proc1972/proc_1081_1972.html (listed 2026-11-19).

metadata.licence: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, BetterGov.ph; adapted for Kuya J with permission

title: EDSA People Power Revolution (22–25 February 1986)
content:
22–25 February 1986: EDSA People Power Revolution. Large civilian demonstrations, following a disputed presidential election and the withdrawal of support by key military officials, led to a change in government. Corazon C. Aquino took office on February 25, and Ferdinand E. Marcos left the country.
Source: https://ncca.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/PHILIPPINE-HISTORY-SOURCE-BOOK-FINAL-SEP022021.pdf (listed 2026-11-19).

title: The 1987 Constitution (1987)
content:
1987: The 1987 Constitution. Ratified in a national plebiscite, the Constitution established the framework for the present presidential system. It provides for a Bill of Rights, three branches of government, constitutional commissions and limits on the exercise of public power.
Source: https://lawphil.net/consti/cons1987.html (listed 2026-11-19).

title: Local Government Code (1991)
content:
1991: Local Government Code. Republic Act No. 7160 transferred specified functions, responsibilities and resources to local governments. It remains a central framework for how provinces, cities, municipalities and barangays deliver public services.
Source: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra1991/ra_7160_1991.html (listed 2026-11-19).

metadata.licence: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, BetterGov.ph; adapted for Kuya J with permission

title: Establishment of BARMM (2019)
content:
2019: Establishment of BARMM. Following plebiscites on the Bangsamoro Organic Law, the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao replaced the ARMM. The law provides for a parliamentary regional government within the Philippine constitutional system.
Source: https://lawphil.net/statutes/repacts/ra2018/ra_11054_2018.html (listed 2026-11-19).
